title: Status page transparency — customer requests roundup (CS)
content:
Owner: Jasmine (CS)
Last updated: 2025-11-21
Audience: SRE/Infra leadership + Product Console/Rollouts + Support Ops
Why this doc exists: consolidate recurring customer asks (enterprise + high-usage self-serve) about our public status page accuracy/granularity and incident communications. This is intended to feed PM-611/PM-612 scope and inform templates + rollout.

---

1) Executive summary (what customers keep asking for)

A. "Your status page is too coarse" (most common)
- Customers want component-level breakdown by capability (Chat vs Streaming vs Embeddings vs Rerank) AND by region.
- The top complaint pattern is: one capability has a user-visible issue (often embeddings or streaming disconnects), but the status page shows “API Operational” so they assume the problem is on their side.

B. Faster time-to-first-update + consistent update cadence
- Enterprise customers explicitly ask for an expectation (e.g., first public update within X minutes of internal declaration; then updates every Y minutes while impact persists).
- They prefer an “Investigating” update even when root cause is unknown, as long as it is clear what is known/unknown.

C. Publishable post-incident summaries
- Customers (and procurement/security teams) want a consistent summary format: impact, timeline, root cause category, mitigations applied, and prevention/follow-ups.
- They do NOT ask for internal hostnames, customer names, or sensitive capacity details. They do ask for clarity about “what failed” and “what changed to prevent recurrence.”

D. Dedicated/Private visibility guidance (less frequent, high stakes)
- Customers don’t necessarily want all Dedicated/Private incidents on the public page, but they want clear rules about:
  - what will be reflected publicly vs communicated privately
  - what Dedicated control-plane signals mean on the status page (if shown)
  - how to interpret partial-region issues ("is this us-east only?")

---

2) Customer request themes (with examples)

Theme 1: Capability-specific components (Embeddings is the #1 gap in tickets)
What they say:
- “Embeddings failed for 40 minutes but status page said everything was fine.”
- “We only use streaming; don’t mark the entire API as down, but do tell us streaming is degraded.”

Why it matters:
- Reduces wasted debugging on the customer side.
- Reduces support load + escalations (customers open Sev2/Sev1 tickets when status is ambiguous).

References:
- SUP-28411 (status page missing embeddings component)
- Slack #support 1759934022: multiple tickets with “status says ok but embeddings failing”

Theme 2: Region-level granularity (us-east and eu-west are the most cited)
What they say:
- “We’re only in us-east; if it’s ap-southeast, we don’t need to page our team.”
- “If it’s us-east only, we can fail over to eu-west — but we need confirmation quickly.”

Why it matters:
- Enables customers with multi-region setups to make faster failover decisions.
- Prevents overreaction (paging the whole org for a region they don’t use).

References:
- SUP-28436 (disputed status accuracy during us-east degradation)
- Fireflies 2025-11-14 QBR follow-up: explicit ask for per-region component visibility

Theme 3: Partial outage vs degraded performance definitions
What they say:
- “Is this errors or latency? We can tolerate slower responses but not 5xx.”
- “Streaming ‘degraded’ needs to map to something we can correlate (disconnects/timeouts).”

Why it matters:
- Customers calibrate mitigation differently based on error vs latency.
- Helps customers validate if they are still affected (especially during mitigation/monitoring).

References:
- SUP-28549 (streaming disconnect spikes not reflected on status)
- Fireflies 2025-11-20 security review: questions about how incidents are declared + what ‘degraded’ means

Theme 4: Status page accuracy disputes (what triggers escalation)
Common triggers:
- Customer has logs showing elevated errors but status page is “Operational”.
- Status page is “Degraded” but customer sees no impact and questions trustworthiness.

What they ask for:
- Evidence that we have objective criteria (dashboards/thresholds) and a process.
- A clear escalation path when they believe status is wrong.

References:
- SUP-28436 (customer disputes status accuracy)
- Slack #support 1759939118 (macro drafting: respond to status accuracy disputes)

---

3) Specific accounts / sales blockers (sanitized notes)

Northbridge AI Platform (enterprise eval)
- Repeated theme: procurement wants predictable incident comms expectations; status page component granularity called out as a vendor comparison item.
- Ask: "Show streaming separately and by region. Provide post-incident summaries we can forward internally."
- References: HubSpot company-northbridge-ai-platform; Fireflies 2025-11-06 procurement call transcript

Lattice Financial (Dedicated prospect)
- Blockers: wants clarity on Dedicated vs public reporting, and how quickly they’ll be notified + what format.
- Ask: published policy for post-incident summaries + a sample.
- References: HubSpot company-lattice-financial

Note: We should assume this becomes table-stakes for enterprise procurement in 2026 (security reviews increasingly treat status/incident comms as part of vendor risk).

---

4) What CS/Support needs from the project (requirements)

CS requirement R1 — Component taxonomy customers can understand
- Plain-language definitions (no internal service names).
- Capability split at minimum: Hosted API (non-streaming requests), Streaming, Embeddings, Reranking.
- Region split at minimum: us-east, us-west, eu-west (others as roadmap). If we can’t do all regions Day 1, we need to clearly label what’s covered.

CS requirement R2 — Comms templates with safe defaults
- “Investigating” should include: what we’re seeing, which components/regions may be affected, and next update timing.
- “Identified” should include: what we believe is happening (without over-precision), mitigation underway.
- “Mitigating/Monitoring” should avoid premature “fixed” language.
- “Resolved” should include: impact window and any customer action required (usually none).

CS requirement R3 — A publishable post-incident summary format
- Must be safe for wide distribution (no customer-specific capacity constraints; no naming specific customers).
- Must answer: impact, duration, affected components/regions, root cause class (category), mitigations, prevention.

CS requirement R4 — A dispute/escalation playbook + macros
- When a customer says “status page wrong,” Support needs:
  - quick steps to validate (which dashboards to check)
  - escalation path to SRE
  - a macro that acknowledges their evidence and commits to follow-up (without admitting fault prematurely)

---

5) Suggested success metrics (CS perspective)

Primary (customer-facing outcomes)
- Reduced tickets with “status says operational but we see failures” as root complaint.
- Improved customer-reported trust in status page (qualitative; tracked in QBR notes).

Operational (CS/Support workload)
- Ticket deflection: fewer duplicative tickets during incidents once accurate components are updated.
- Faster Support triage time during incidents (time-to-classify: “known incident vs customer-specific issue”).

Suggested measurement approach
- Tag support tickets during incidents with: status_accuracy_dispute / status_granularity_request / post_incident_summary_request.
- Compare volume pre vs post rollout (4-week windows).

---

6) Open questions / watch-outs

1) Dedicated/Private public reporting
- Customers vary: some want everything public; others prefer private comms only.
- Proposed stance (CS): public status page should show broad platform components (Hosted API capabilities + regions). Dedicated/Private should be handled via account comms with optional high-level public notice only when there is broad impact.
- Action: align on policy language for PM-612.

2) Avoid over-promising SLAs
- Several customers asked for “update within 15 minutes” explicitly.
- We should avoid hard commitments on the public status page unless we can consistently hit them; better to use targets (“aim to provide an update within…”) and track internally.

3) Avoid false positives / flapping
- Customers hate when status toggles repeatedly; they interpret it as lack of control.
- Anti-flap rules and clear thresholds are important for trust, even if it means we’re slower to declare very transient spikes.

---

7) Next steps (requested from SRE/PM)

By end of Week 1 of implementation:
- Confirm component list that will be visible Day 1 (capabilities + initial regions).
- Confirm policy stance for Dedicated/Private incidents (public vs private).

Before limited public rollout:
- Provide Support/CS macros aligned to templates (Dev/Support Ops owning).
- Provide 1–2 example post-incident summaries that are “publish-ready” (sanitized) for enterprise sharing.

Points of contact:
- CS: Jasmine Liu (owner), Rachel Kim
- Support Ops: Dev Patel, Owen Phillips
- Customer-facing language: Wei Chen

Appendix A — Ticket snippets (quick reference)
- SUP-28411: enterprise customer explicitly requests embeddings listed as separate component; claims they spent ~2 hours debugging client-side due to status page mismatch.
- SUP-28549: streaming disconnect spike; customer requests streaming-specific incident flag + more precise region tagging.
- SUP-28502: request for consistent post-incident summary format that can be forwarded internally (security + compliance stakeholders).
